rics.meaning: External Debt: Banks — Indonesian banks' foreign-currency borrowings (interbank lines, syndications, FX bonds).
rics.how_to_use: ~$50B. Banks fund their FX loan books via FX deposits + external borrowing. Watch for sudden surges as a sign of dollar funding squeezes. Indonesian regulator (OJK) caps banks' foreign-currency net open positions to limit FX risk.

rics.meaning: External Debt: General Government — the central + sub-national government foreign debt component. Closely tracks aIDCGVXA with minor methodological differences.
rics.how_to_use: Use for cross-validation against aIDCGVXA. The 'general government' framing aligns with IMF/SDDS reporting standards. Sub-national (provincial, regency) external debt is small in Indonesia — central government dominates.

rics.meaning: External Debt: Monetary Authorities — Bank Indonesia's foreign liabilities (IMF SDR allocation, FX swap lines, etc.).
rics.how_to_use: Small. Includes BI's bilateral swap lines (with PBOC, BoJ, etc.) and IMF allocations. Activated swaps appear here.

rics.meaning: External Debt: Other Sectors — non-financial corporate external debt. Includes USD/EUR bonds issued by SOEs (Pertamina, PLN) and private corporates, plus offshore loans.
rics.how_to_use: ~$200B. State-owned enterprises (PLN, Pertamina) account for a large share — their FX bonds are quasi-sovereign. Watch corporate refinancing schedules around major maturities; FX-mismatched corporates are the EM-stress vulnerability point.

rics.meaning: External Debt, Total (SDDS-sourced) — IMF Special Data Dissemination Standard external-debt total.
rics.how_to_use: Cross-check against aIDCEXTA. SDDS-format aligns with international debt-statistics standards.

rics.description: Government External Debt, % quarter on quarter, Standardized, Chg P/P
rics.meaning: Government External Debt, QoQ absolute change — change in government foreign debt level.
rics.how_to_use: Tracks Treasury's foreign-currency funding cadence. Indonesia's typical pattern: USD/EUR/JPY bond issuance front-loaded in Q1.

rics.description: Government External Debt, % year on year, Standardized, Chg Y/Y
rics.meaning: Government External Debt, YoY change — pace of government external-borrowing growth.
rics.how_to_use: Track for sovereign-financing cycle. Indonesia gov external debt YoY growth typically 5-10%; surges during fiscal-stress years (2020 COVID).

rics.meaning: Government External Debt — central government's foreign-currency debt + non-resident-held SBN. Largest single component of total external debt.
rics.how_to_use: Indonesia government external debt ~$200B. Decompose: bilateral/multilateral loans (~$50B, mostly USD/JPY) + global bonds (~$80B in USD, EUR, JPY, samurai) + non-resident SBN holdings (~$70B). Foreign-currency portion is the FX-risk concern; non-resident SBN is the flow-risk concern (sudden outflows).

rics.description: Total External Debt, % quarter on quarter, Standardized, Chg P/P
rics.meaning: Total External Debt, QoQ absolute change — change in external debt level vs prior quarter.
rics.how_to_use: Track for borrowing cycle. Sharp QoQ surges (>$10B) signal aggressive external borrowing.

rics.description: Total External Debt, % year on year, Standardized, Chg Y/Y
rics.meaning: Total External Debt, year-over-year change — pace of external-debt accumulation or paydown.
rics.how_to_use: Track for external-vulnerability buildup. Sustained >10% YoY growth signals over-borrowing in foreign currency. Indonesia ran 8-12% YoY growth pre-COVID (driven by infrastructure financing); recent growth slower (~3-5%). Spike in YoY rate alongside IDR weakness flags refinancing stress.

rics.meaning: Total External Debt — debt owed to non-residents in foreign currencies + IDR-denominated debt held by foreigners. Published quarterly by Bank Indonesia (SULNI report).
rics.how_to_use: Indonesia's external debt ~$415B (2024). Composition: ~50% government, ~25% banks, ~25% non-financial corporates. Compare to FX reserves (~$140B) and exports (~$300B) for adequacy gauges. External debt to GDP ~30% — moderate but rising.
